title: Revisiting Automated Quantum Periodic Distinguisher Construction
abstract: Simon's algorithm can detect hidden XOR periods in functions derived from symmetric ciphers. Finding such functions becomes difficult when nonlinear layers and diffusion spread the relevant expressions across many branches, so recent work has used symbolic search to automate the construction. We refine the algebraic SMT model of Liu et al. in two ways. Prefix realization checks whether a symbolic starting state can be reached through preceding rounds and records the round-key nibbles needed to produce it. DDT Filtering restricts a local S-box input to a DDT bucket so that the symbolic path can cross an additional nonlinear layer. The latter condition is key-dependent: the target period need not lie in the translation space of the selected bucket, and our results state this condition explicitly. We report the maximum round counts found for GFS-2F, GFS-4F, Skipjack-B, LBlock, TWINE, CRAFT, and SKINNY, with Liu et al.'s automated model as the main comparison. We also combine selected witnesses with partial round-key guesses in the Grover–meet–Simon setting, yielding reduced-round key-recovery candidates below the corresponding comparison budgets.

        difficult when nonlinear layers and diffusion spread the relevant expres-
        sions across many branches, so recent work has used symbolic search to
        automate the construction. We refine the algebraic SMT model of Liu
        et al. in two ways. Prefix realization checks whether a symbolic starting
        state can be reached through preceding rounds and records the round-

        input to a DDT bucket so that the symbolic path can cross an addi-
        tional nonlinear layer. The latter condition is key-dependent: the tar-
        get period need not lie in the translation space of the selected bucket,
        and our results state this condition explicitly. We report the maximum
        round counts found for GFS-2F, GFS-4F, Skipjack-B, LBlock, TWINE,
        CRAFT, and SKINNY, with Liu et al.’s automated model as the main

        Keywords: Quantum periodic distinguishers · SMT-based tools


1     Introduction
In discussions of the quantum threat to symmetric cryptography, Grover’s algo-
rithm is often taken as the default reference point. It is a quantum algorithm for
unstructured search, and in the symmetric setting it gives a quadratic speedup
for exhaustive key search. Quantum security is therefore often viewed mainly
as a question of key length [12]. This Grover-based baseline, however, does not
fully capture the quantum attack surface relevant to symmetric cryptography.
Simon’s algorithm is designed to recover a hidden period in a structured func-
tion. In the present setting, the relevant case is a hidden XOR period induced
by a cryptographic construction. Once such a structure is present, Simon’s algo-
rithm can test for or recover the period in polynomial time in the stated oracle
model [26]. From this viewpoint, quantum symmetric security depends both on
the margin against quantum search and on the presence of exploitable structure
that a quantum adversary can query and use.
    The line of Simon-based symmetric cryptanalysis is by now well established.
Early works on reduced-round Feistel and Even–Mansour style constructions
2      Jian Guo and Yiran Yao

showed how cipher structure can create the hidden periods used by these attacks
[18,19], and Santoli and Schaffner later systematized this attack perspective on
symmetric primitives [25]. At CRYPTO 2016, Kaplan et al. then demonstrated
attacks on widely used symmetric constructions under quantum query access
[16]. Subsequent advances broadened both scope and technique, including the
Grover–meet–Simon paradigm of Leander and May [20], the Offline Simon refine-
ments of Bonnetain et al. [4], and quantum linearization attacks on parallelizable
constructions [5]. Simon-based attacks should therefore be viewed as a structural
attack family in their own right.
    The central practical difficulty is the construction of a function to which Si-
mon’s algorithm can be applied. For small Feistel settings, suitable periodic dis-
tinguishers can often be derived directly [18,15]. The situation changes on higher-
branch generalized Feistel networks and on more diffusive designs, where the
literature contains many carefully engineered, cipher-specific or family-specific
constructions [11,10,13,22,8,9,27]. In these richer settings, the difficulty is to
preserve the structural constraints that support periodicity as propagation be-
comes more entangled. As branch interactions accumulate, constants interfere
with clean cancellation patterns, and unknown differences propagate rapidly,
the symbolic invariants that make low-complexity examples tractable become
much harder to preserve. The bottleneck is therefore to turn periodic-function
construction into a systematic search procedure rather than a collection of hand-
crafted examples. SPN-style block ciphers, represented in our experiments by
SKINNY [1] and CRAFT [2], are a complementary test. Their nonlinear and
linear layers quickly spread unknown differences to many cells. The coarse sym-
bolic model then loses useful information after only a few rounds.
    Existing work addresses this bottleneck from several complementary angles.
One line gives structural conditions for Simon-compatible relations, beginning
with separability-style viewpoints and their stronger variants [14,31]. A second
line tests generalized Simon conditions by enumerating circuits [6]. A third line
connects Simon-based distinguishers to truncated differentials, thereby clarifying
how quantum periodicity can sometimes be read through more classical prop-
agation arguments [30]; recent simplified searches push this bridge further on
selected families [7]. Liu et al. instead use algebraic representations of Feistel
branches in an SMT model [21]. These are distinct forms of automation: the
algebraic model does not subsume every construction found by circuit enumer-
ation. Our work starts from Liu et al.’s model and adds two specific checks
motivated by differential propagation.
    This paper takes the recent symbolic model of Liu et al. as the comparison
point [21]. Our experiments compare the maximum round counts found by the
two automated models. They are not claims of the best known distinguishers or
key-recovery attacks on the listed ciphers. We also test whether selected witnesses
can be combined with partial round-key guesses while keeping the estimated
Grover–meet–Simon work below the stated comparison budget.

1.1   Our Contributions

First, prefix realization checks whether a symbolic suffix boundary B can be
produced after p preceding rounds. When it can, the procedure records the input
expressions and the required round-key nibbles. Integrating this check into the
search makes it possible to compare longer paths under one global complexity
limit; the underlying idea of guessing early-round key material is not new.
    Second, DDT Filtering restricts a local nonlinear input to a selected DDT
bucket. This can preserve a useful symbolic value for one more nonlinear step.
The retained bucket supports the intended period only when the key-dependent
period s lies in its translation space V . We state this condition and its probability
separately instead of assuming that it always holds.
    Third, we evaluate the two changes on generalized-Feistel, Skipjack-type,
lightweight balanced, and SPN-style targets. The tables report symbolic paths,
the required events along those paths, and the maximum round counts found.
A path with W > 0 is conditional on s(K) ∈ V ; it is not by itself a complete
distinguisher for every key.
    Finally, an automated p + s + a search combines selected witnesses with the
round-key nibbles needed before the periodic path and for partial decryption
after it. The resulting rows give candidate-search estimates. They do not use the
key schedule to recover the full master key.
    Table 1 summarizes the main differences from the symbolic model of Liu et al.
The Base row is their result. The Prefix-realization row reports connected prefix–
suffix paths for p = 1, 2, 3, 4. The DDT Filtering row reports symbolic suffix
paths with the local filter enabled. For CRAFT, round counts follow the official
convention: a searched core trail of length r is reported as r + 1 CRAFT rounds.
The evaluated targets cover GFS-2F and GFS-4F as generalized-Feistel struc-
tures [24], a Skipjack-type structure following the Skipjack analysis of Knud-
sen and Wagner [17], and the concrete block ciphers LBlock [29], TWINE [28],
CRAFT [2], and SKINNY [1]. In all GFS experiments reported here, one cell is
instantiated as 4 bits.


1.2   Organization

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. After the preliminaries in
Section 2, Section 3 presents the inherited symbolic model, input-domain exten-
sion via prefix realization, DDT Filtering, and the event probabilities used later.
Section 4 evaluates the resulting distinguisher-level witnesses through prefix-
realization and DDT Filtering experiments. Section 5 combines selected wit-
nesses with partial round-key guesses in Grover–meet–Simon style key-recovery
candidates, including the complexity rule, full-search automation, execution pro-
cedure, and final rows. Section 6 concludes the paper.

2     Preliminaries
2.1   Notation
Let
                               E r : {0, 1}N → {0, 1}N
denote the r-round version of the target cipher or public permutation. When
the state is partitioned into t branches of n bits, we write N = tn and denote
the round function in round i by fi . For a designated branch, or more generally
a designated set of output coordinates, we write E r |u for the corresponding
projection. This notation is sufficient for all later constructions.
    As in the Simon-based distinguisher literature [30,21], inputs will be decom-
posed as (x, αb , c), where b ∈ {0, 1}, x ∈ {0, 1}n is the variable part, α0 ̸= α1
are fixed constants, and c collects the remaining fixed coordinates. We write
δ = α0 ⊕ α1 and reserve s ̸= 0 for a hidden XOR period. A typical periodic
distinguisher is obtained by constructing a function of the form
                       g(x) = E r (x, α0 , c)|u ⊕ E r (x, α1 , c)|u
and then showing that g hides a nontrivial period together with suitable control
of spurious collisions.

2.2   Simon’s Algorithm
Simon showed that a hidden XOR period can be found in polynomial time from
quantum oracle access [26]. Concretely, for a function g : {0, 1}n → {0, 1}m , if
there exists s ̸= 0 such that g(x) = g(x⊕s) for all x, and if collisions not explained
by s remain sufficiently sparse, then O(n) quantum queries yield linear relations
orthogonal to s, from which the period is recovered with high probability. For
the present paper, this standard consequence is the only property of Simon’s
algorithm that is needed: once a cipher-induced function is shown to hide a
period, Simon turns that structure into a polynomial-time quantum test.
    In the cryptanalytic line initiated by Kaplan et al. [16], however, Simon is
often used in a weaker, distinguisher-oriented sense. The objective need not be
the explicit recovery of s. It is enough that the measurement outcomes pro-
duced by Simon’s procedure are confined to a proper subspace, since a gen-
uine hidden period forces every sample y to satisfy y · s = 0, whereas under a
random-permutation view the samples span the full n-dimensional space with
overwhelming probability. This viewpoint is already explicit in the Simon-based
distinguisher literature, including the Feistel attacks of Ito et al. [15], and it is
the interpretation adopted throughout this paper whenever we say that Simon’s
algorithm applies.

2.3   Grover–Meet–Simon
Leander and May introduced the Grover–meet–Simon method for settings in
which periodicity becomes visible only after guessing an auxiliary value [20]. In
6       Jian Guo and Yiran Yao

its basic form, one considers a function h(u, x) such that only the correct outer
guess u∗ makes the partial function x 7→ h(u∗ , x) hide a nontrivial period. Grover
search then explores the outer guess space, while Simon serves as the inner test
that recognizes whether the corresponding partial function is periodic. Bonnetain
et al. refined this method and its complexity analysis in later work [4].
    We use Grover–meet–Simon only as an outer complexity wrapper. When a
periodic relation appears only after guessing some intermediate value or key-
dependent quantity in a space of size 2m , the later key-recovery analysis will
account for the attack cost as Grover search over that space, up to polynomial
factors coming from oracle evaluation and the inner Simon routine. No further
detail is needed here.
    The Grover–meet–Simon costs used later are stated in the Q2 model. The
inner Simon test requires coherent superposition access to x 7→ h(u, x) for each
outer guess u. With only Q1 access, the adversary obtains classical oracle data
instead; using such data requires a separate offline-Simon conversion [4] and
separate data/time accounting. Consequently, the O(2 e m/2 poly(n)) bounds used
here do not directly apply in the Q1 model. Within Q2, our default access model
is qCPA, namely superposition chosen-plaintext access. We use qCCA only when
a construction requires superposition access to the inverse oracle; local reversible
computation under guessed outer-round values does not by itself require such
access.

2.4   Link to Truncated Differentials
An important conceptual step in this area is the observation of Xiang et al. that
many Simon-based periodic distinguishers admit a truncated-differential inter-
pretation [30]. In the present notation, one studies two related inputs (x, α0 , c)
and (x, α1 , c) and asks whether, after a suitable number of rounds, the projected
output difference on u behaves periodically in x. If so, the function

                      g(x) = E r (x, α0 , c)|u ⊕ E r (x, α1 , c)|u

inherits a hidden period and becomes a valid target for Simon’s algorithm. The
truncated-differential viewpoint is useful because it identifies which coordinates
must remain fixed, which may vary, and where cancellation occurs in the pro-
jected output.
    For the purposes of this paper, however, this bridge is only a sufficient mecha-
nism, not a complete characterization of useful periodic constructions. It is most
transparent when the relevant propagation can be captured by tractable trun-
cated differences, as in several Feistel and generalized-Feistel examples [30]. The
settings considered later are less benign: unknown differences, stronger diffu-
sion, and interactions across several branches may still permit periodic behavior
even when no direct truncated-differential formulation is available. The next sec-
tion therefore moves from this bridge to the more general symbolic-construction
methodology that underlies the search model of Liu et al. [21] and the refine-
ments developed in this paper.

3     Baseline Model and Our Modifications
3.1   Periodic-Distinguisher Search Target
Before describing the SMT model, we recall the path property that the model
is designed to find. Write the two related inputs as
                               (x, α0 , c),      (x, α1 , c),
where x is the query variable, α0 , α1 are two fixed constants, c collects the
remaining fixed coordinates, and δ = α0 ⊕ α1 . For a selected output coordinate
u, the periodic-distinguisher function has the form
                       g(x) = E r (x, α0 , c)|u ⊕ E r (x, α1 , c)|u .
   The useful endpoint condition is that the projected output still contains a
separable dependence on x and αb . Liu et al. call this the differential separability
property. A typical sufficient form is
             E r (x, αb , c)|u = F (x ⊕ G(αb , c), c) ⊕ P (x, c) ⊕ Q(αb , c).
In the difference defining g(x), the term P (x, c) cancels and Q(αb , c) contributes
only a fixed difference. The remaining F -term has period
                               s = G(α0 , c) ⊕ G(α1 , c),
because shifting x by s swaps the two inputs to F . Hence g(x ⊕ s) = g(x).
    The symbolic search does not reconstruct this algebraic expression in full.
Instead, it tracks whether a path preserves enough structure to certify such an
endpoint. In the inherited model, this is represented by an output branch that
is either separable, denoted 0s, or still directly related to the x-family variable.
The rest of this section describes the symbolic abstraction and constraints used
to search for such paths.

3.2   The Inherited Baseline as a Control Setting
We now describe the inherited SMT model used as the control setting. For a
fixed round wiring and round count, the model asks whether there is a symbolic
path from an allowed input pattern to one of the endpoint forms described above.
The starting point is the algebraic SMT model of Liu et al. [21]. It represents
the values of Feistel branches algebraically. Canale et al. [6] instead enumerate
circuits that satisfy generalized Simon conditions. The two approaches are re-
lated but distinct: the model of Liu et al. is not a simple extension of circuit
enumeration and does not contain all of its constructions.
    The solver takes three kinds of input. The first is the round wiring, writ-
ten only with the three generic operations Split, R, and Xor. The second is
the symbolic domain allowed at the input branches. The third is a set of global
budgets on constrained events. A satisfiable instance returns a valid input as-
signment, the symbolic state of every intermediate branch, and the event flags
activated along the path. An unsatisfiable instance means that no valid path
exists under the same wiring, domain, and budgets.

Symbolic states. To keep the search tractable, the baseline does not track full
algebraic expressions on each branch. Instead, each branch is assigned a coarse

Internally, this is a component-wise Boolean encoding rather than a one-hot

3.3   Forward Extension: Adding Prefix Rounds with Accounted

The inherited abstraction is designed to search symbolic suffix paths. It starts
from an allowed input pattern, propagates the coarse states through the round
wiring, and checks whether the final state still contains a usable x-related or
separable branch. Its input alphabet is only

                                  {0, x, δ, x ⊕ δ}.

This is sufficient when the state at the beginning of the path can already be
written in this alphabet. Prefix realization asks an additional question: can this

    This example motivates the boundary terminology used below. The prefix-
suffix boundary is the state where the added prefix rounds meet the symbolic

The symbol Fi (x) says that the x-dependent value has passed through a specific
local round-function instance before the suffix starts. In this view, the input-side

to expressions such as

This notation explains why the old input alphabet is too small, but it is not
a good representation for longer prefixes. After two or more preceding rounds,
the input-side expressions can contain nested local functions, XORs of several
branches, and several key-mixed values. Treating all of these as new coarse sym-
bols would hide the required round-key cells. Therefore, the prefix is not folded
into the suffix alphabet. The suffix remains symbolic, while the prefix is handled
as an expression-construction problem.
    For a fixed prefix length p, the construction starts from a selected prefix-
suffix boundary and walks backward through the p preceding rounds. Copy edges
simply copy the required expression to the predecessor wire. For an Xor update,
the rule is the usual algebraic rearrangement: if the forward update contains
                                 v ′ = a ⊕ Fr,i (b),
and the boundary requires a particular expression for v ′ , then one predecessor
expression can be chosen by setting
                                 a = v ′ ⊕ Fr,i (b).
The local nonlinear function is not inverted; it is kept as a named key-dependent
function inside the expression. Wires that are not needed by the chosen path are
fixed to constants. The constructed input-side expressions are then forwarded
through the same p rounds to check that they reach the selected prefix-suffix
boundary.
    The prefix can be used in two ways. In a prefix-only scan, the search enumer-
ates possible prefix-suffix boundaries and asks how many preceding rounds can
produce them, together with the minimum number of round-key cells needed. In
the key-recovery candidate search, the suffix solver first determines the actual
suffix starting state used by a p + s + a decomposition; the same prefix construc-
tion is then applied to that state. Thus the prefix changes which suffix starting

4.4   Distinguisher-Level Synthesis
The two refinements expose different sources of additional distinguisher rounds.
Prefix realization enlarges the effective input domain by realizing an internal
suffix boundary through a short keyed prefix. It therefore converts some paths
that are invisible from the inherited plaintext-level input language into valid
distinguisher witnesses. DDT Filtering acts later, inside the suffix, by paying for
one local DDT-controlled propagation when the ordinary symbolic transition
would lose the useful x-family structure.
    The tables also show why the two refinements should be evaluated by ci-
pher family rather than by a single aggregate number. Generalized-Feistel and
Skipjack-type wirings preserve narrow branch paths, so prefix realization and
local filtering translate directly into longer paths. LBlock and TWINE show a
second effect: even when the maximum symbolic suffix is expensive, DDT Filter-
ing can reduce the collision burden at a fixed round count. CRAFT and SKINNY
show the SPN-side behavior, where full-state diffusion changes the required con-
ditions because one local filtered transition is quickly mixed with many other
active cells.
    Relative to the baseline symbolic search of Liu et al. [21], the refined model
therefore does more than report a larger maximum round count. It records which
additional witnesses come from input-domain extension, which come from suffix-
side DDT Filtering, and what required events are introduced by each mechanism.
The next section uses selected witnesses from this evaluation in a key-recovery
candidate search with input-side and partial-decryption round-key guesses.


5     From Distinguishers to Key-Recovery Candidates

Section 4 reports periodic-distinguisher witnesses produced by the refined sym-
bolic search. This section explains how selected witnesses are combined with
partial round-key guesses in a Grover–meet–Simon search. A distinguisher row
contains a symbolic path and the probabilities assigned to its required events. A
key-recovery candidate also specifies the round-key nibbles needed before that
path and for partial decryption after it. The search returns candidates only for

5.1   Combining the Three Parts
A periodic-distinguisher witness specifies an internal boundary, a suffix path,
a target output coordinate, and the required events used by the path. A key-
recovery candidate connects this witness to plaintext and ciphertext. We write
the total number of rounds as

                                   R = p + s + a,

where p prefix rounds realize the suffix boundary from input-side expressions,
s rounds are covered by the symbolic suffix path, and a output-side rounds are
peeled from the ciphertext under guessed key material.
    The result is not monotone in the suffix length. A path that gives a longer
periodic distinguisher can still fail as a key-recovery candidate if the prefix real-
ization or partial decryption requires too many round-key nibbles. For the latter,
the implementation starts from the internal target coordinate and expands its
dependencies forward through the a appended rounds toward the ciphertext. It
records every branch and round-key nibble needed to compute that target from
the ciphertext and the guessed values. The full search therefore considers the
whole p + s + a split, not the suffix length alone.

5.2   Recorded Data and Complexity
A searched row has the form

                          M = (p, s, a, B, τ, R, Ein , Cout ).

Here B is the suffix input boundary, τ is the target output coordinate, and
R is the symbolic suffix path, including its collision events and DDT Filtering
events. The object Ein records the input-side expressions that realize B after the
first p rounds. The object Cout records the dependencies and round-key nibbles
needed to partially decrypt the last a rounds to τ . Let Kfwd and Kout be the
two corresponding key-component supports, and let Kfwd and Kout denote their
individual sizes.
    For the 4-bit-cell searches, the exponent of the required suffix events is

                                   P = 4X + 4W,

where X is the number of charged collision events and W is the number of DDT
Filtering events. Events that force a useful zero output shape determine the
symbolic path but add no probability term. The number of guessed round-key
bits is computed from the union of the two supports:

                              G = bits(Kfwd ∪ Kout ) .

exhaustively at low classical cost; Grover–meet–Simon instead searches the re-

    Across the 4-bit-cell rows, required round-key cells are measured in 4-bit
units. Thus one required key-mixed S-box input contributes 4 guessed bits, one
charged X-collision contributes a 4-bit condition, and one DDT Filtering event
contributes a 4-bit condition. The columns Kfwd and Kout report the input-side
and partial-decryption support sizes selected by the search, and G counts the
distinct guessed bits in their union. For example, the TWINE-80 supports are

5.3   Automated Candidate Search
The search combines the prefix, suffix, and partial-decryption analyses in one
loop. The suffix path is the structural core of the candidate: it fixes the bound-
ary B, the target coordinate τ , and the event counts X, W . The prefix and
partial-decryption checks then decide whether this path can be connected to
plaintext and ciphertext under the comparison budget. The prefix check de-
termines whether B is reachable and records the required round-key nibbles.
Starting at τ , the partial-decryption check expands dependencies toward the ci-
phertext through the appended rounds and records the additional nibbles. Only
then is G + P < κ tested. A W > 0 template is marked conditional.
    The implementation is suffix-first because the periodic structure is created
inside the suffix. Once a suffix witness is found, the same boundary is passed
to the prefix-realization routine, which reconstructs input-side expressions and
records the round-key nibbles needed to instantiate them. The target coordinate
is passed to the partial-decryption routine, which expands its forward dependen-
cies through the appended rounds and records the nibbles needed to evaluate the
target from the ciphertext. The two supports are merged before the guessed-bit

6   Conclusion
This paper studied the automated construction of quantum periodic distinguish-
ers for block-cipher structures. Starting from the algebraic SMT model of Liu et
al., we added checks that connect an internal symbolic path to preceding rounds
and that condition one nonlinear step on a DDT bucket. Our main comparison is
with that automated model; the results are not claims of the best known attacks
on the listed ciphers.
     The main methodological additions are input-domain extension via prefix
realization and DDT Filtering. Prefix realization determines whether an internal
suffix boundary can be produced from input-side expressions, and records the
round-key nibbles needed by that realization. DDT Filtering adds a controlled
local suffix event based on a DDT-compatible transition through a nonlinear
component. The target period does not necessarily lie in the translation space
of the selected bucket. We therefore state every W > 0 numerical result as
conditional on the membership event s(K) ∈ V ; W = 0 rows are unaffected.
     At the distinguisher level, the experiments show how these refinements be-
have across several cipher families. For the generalized-Feistel and Skipjack-type
structures, the refined model finds longer symbolic periodic paths. For TWINE
and LBlock, the results give parallel 4-bit Feistel-like profiles under the same
corrected symbolic rules. For CRAFT and SKINNY, the experiments show how
stronger SPN-style diffusion changes the balance between longer paths and the
conditions needed to realize or filter them. The experiments separate input real-
ization, local filtering, and collision conditions so that the source of each change
can be checked directly.
     We also combined selected witnesses with the round-key nibbles required
before the periodic path and for partial decryption after it. The candidate-search
estimate includes collision and filtering conditions. When W > 0, it is conditional
on s(K) ∈ V . These rows search only for candidates for the listed round-key
material; full master-key recovery through the key schedule is outside the paper.
